hints: Notice the recommendation pairs a longer extension cord for the drill with a bigger cross-sectional area to keep the cord resistance low.
Recall the resistivity relation $R = \rho L / A$ for a wire of length $L$ and area $A$.
Check how $R$ changes if $L$ is increased, then decide how $A$ must change to bring $R$ back down to a similar value.
walkthrough: The cord should add as little resistance as possible so most of the supply voltage reaches the drill and little power is lost as heat in the cord.
The governing rule is $R = \rho L / A$, where $\rho$ is the resistivity of the cord material.
Increasing the length $L$ increases $R$ in direct proportion, so a longer extension cord on its own would have higher resistance.
Increasing the cross-sectional area $A$ decreases $R$ in inverse proportion, because there is more conducting material in parallel.
To offset the rise in $R$ from a larger $L$, $A$ must also be made larger to keep $R$ about the same.
That dependence is resistance proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. This is option D

options.A: Resistance increases when the cord length increases, so it cannot be inversely proportional to length.
options.B: This reverses both dependences, since a longer cord increases resistance and a thicker cord decreases resistance.
options.C: Resistance does increase with length, but a larger cross-sectional area decreases resistance rather than increasing it.
options.D: From $R = \rho L / A$, a longer $L$ raises $R$ and a larger $A$ lowers $R$, so thicker wire compensates for extra length.
